newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe pledges jobs, "new democracy".
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe pledges jobs, "new democracy".

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, seeking to a unite his fractious coalition for a parliamentary confidence vote on Wednesday, promised a "new democracy" for the year 2000 and a drive for jobs amid record unemployment.

"I believe perseverance will pay off and that 1997 will be a year of improvement," the embattled premier told parliament, urging his allies to combat widespread gloom and convince voters that the centre-right government was on the right track.
Juppe was assured of a huge majority in the evening vote, the third since he took office in May 1995. His centre-right coalition holds four-fifths of the 577 National Assembly seats.

He said his two main priorities for coming months were "to complete, reinforce, energise our strategy for jobs" and "build a new democracy for the citizen of the year 2000" with as yet ill-defined plans to reform the state and the justice system.

Coalition leaders in Juppe's conservative Rally for the Republic (RPR) party and the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF) said they would back Juppe in the vote, despite misgivings about some of Juppe's recent policy initiatives.
"Yes, Mr Prime Minister, you have the confidence of the UDF. In parallel, can you tell us if we, the parliamentarians of the UDF, have yours?" asked UDF floor leader Gilles de Robien.

He pleaded for more consultation with the UDF, the junior coalition partner, in the run-up to the next elections in 1998 and reiterated "reserves" about Juppe's suggestions to reform voting laws and a plan to tighten anti-racism laws.
The opposition Socialist party said France needed a radical shift in policy to bolster economic growth and said the vote was aimed at stifling debate on policy within the ruling coalition.
"We know France needs a change of policy. From now on, everyone will know that to change policy, we must change coalition," said former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius.
Juppe retorted that he was willing to consult his partners. "This vote of confidence will not be a blank check," he said.

Juppe, addressing parliament for the first time since the summer recess, said a rise in unemployment to 12.6 percent of the workforce was "unacceptable". He said he would launch a "new decentralised plan of action for jobs, notably for the young".
In a 30-minute speech, he said the draft 1997 budget would bring public spending under control and put France on target to qualify for a single European Union currency from 1999.
"I'm sure the single currency will be the locomotive for Europe which we need in the world of the 21st century," he said.
Juppe's approval rating is near to an all-time low at 30 percent and President Jacques Chirac had to intervene twice in the last week to shield him from criticism within the coalition.
To strengthen democracy, Juppe said he wanted to simplify the state bureaucracy, involve citizens more in decision-making and strengthen the presumption of innocence in French law.
He said the government would put to parliament soon a bill toughening anti-racism laws to combat "increase in racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic speech and behaviour".

But he hinted he might allow coalition deputies a free vote on the bill, largely aimed at countering extreme-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, by saying: "Everyone will decide according to their beliefs."
Juppe did not press a suggestion last month of adding a dose of proportional representation to the parliamentary system.
He said he would open consultations with political parties next week on issues ranging from the under-representation of women in parliament to voting laws, but he made no proposals of his own.
